<reason>Both sides agreed distrust rose and the euro survived, so the debate turned on whether retained membership counts as "preserved solidarity" and how to weigh it. PRO built the stronger comparative frame: it pocketed CON's early concession, argued that the new instruments (ESM outside treaties, fiscal compact sanctions, stalled deposit insurance) were distrust institutionalized rather than solidarity, and supplied a usable weighing threshold (durability) when pressed. PRO also gave a grounded answer to CON's "name an available alternative" question (2010 restructuring, Ireland's bondholders) that undercut CON's "no other response was possible" counterfactual. CON's case was coherent but rested on a low-bar definition ("nobody left") and a rigged binary counterfactual; its "symmetric shock" explanation for the pandemic fund was plausible but did not fully explain the absence of Troika-style conditionality. CON's "internment" answer to Q1 was turned against it in PRO's closing (Greece 2015 met two of three criteria). PRO's small overreach—claiming CON's "silence" before CON had spoken—costs a little, but the overall route to victory remained PRO's.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A4.1]-[A4.3] answer to CON's threshold question: defining the magnitude test as durability (anger that outlasts recovery, reshapes party systems, and makes the architects refuse to repeat the playbook) and showing solidarity "flatlined" for seven years while distrust compounded—then exploiting CON's own "internment" example in closing to show Greece 2015 nearly met it.</best_rebuttal>
